blocks.md: **Once each variable is described, look at pairs. A scatterplot with both a straight regression line and a lowess smoother is the first test of the linear model: where the two curves part, a straight line misrepresents the relationship. On the Prestige data they part at high incomes, where prestige rises more slowly than the line assumes.**

sections.heading: 1. Scatterplots with a line and a smoother

blocks.md: The lecture plots prestige against income for 102 occupations, with the OLS line (solid, with its confidence band) and a [lowess](note:lowess-smoother) curve (dashed). Lowess fits a weighted line in a moving window around each income level and joins the fitted heights, so it traces the average of $y$ at each $x$ without assuming a shape. The two agree up to incomes of about 10,000, then lowess bends below the line.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Scatterplot with OLS line and lowess - prestige on income.png
blocks.alt: Scatterplot with OLS line and lowess - prestige on income

blocks.prompt: In the lecture's scatterplot of prestige on income, the lowess curve follows the OLS line up to incomes of about 10,000 and then bends below it. What does that say about a straight-line regression of prestige on income?

options.md: Nothing: lowess always bends at the ends because there are few points there
options.feedback: Lowess is less reliable at the extremes, but here the bend starts at about 10,000 and several occupations lie beyond it, all below the straight line.

options.md: The relationship is linear, but the errors are heteroskedastic
options.feedback: A smoother that departs from the line is a statement about the *mean* of prestige at each income, not about its spread.

options.md: Prestige rises more slowly at high incomes, so the line over-predicts prestige for the highest-paid occupations; a concave form such as log income may fit better

blocks.why: Lowess estimates the average prestige at each income locally. Where it lies below the OLS line, the line predicts more prestige than occupations at that income actually have. A curve that flattens as income rises is concave, which is the shape of a log: L5 returns to this choice of functional form.

blocks.prompt: What does a lowess curve compute at a given income level $x_0$?

options.md: The height at $x_0$ of a weighted least-squares line fitted to the observations with incomes near $x_0$, with nearer points weighted more
The average of $y$ over all observations, weighted by how far their $x$ is from the overall mean
options.feedback: That would give one number for every $x_0$. Lowess refits at each $x_0$ using only a window of nearby observations.

options.md: The fitted value from a high-degree polynomial in $x$ estimated on the whole sample
options.feedback: A global polynomial uses every point for every $x_0$, so a few extreme points can bend the whole curve. Lowess is local.

blocks.why: At each $x_0$, lowess takes a share of the data closest to $x_0$, weights them by distance (nearest points count most) and fits a line by weighted least squares; the curve joins the heights of those local lines. Because each piece is local, the curve can bend wherever the data do, which is what makes it a check on the single global line of OLS.

blocks.prompt: Fit a lowess curve by changing its span, and compare it with the OLS line
blocks.purpose: See lowess as many local weighted lines, and see the span trade-off: large span approaches the OLS line, small span chases noise

sections.heading: 2. Grouped scatterplots and the scatterplot matrix

blocks.md: Colouring the same plot by occupation type (professional, white collar, blue collar) and fitting a line to each group shows that the groups sit at different levels and with different slopes: the professional line is the flattest. A scatterplot matrix extends the idea to every pair of prestige, income, education and the share of women, with each variable's distribution by type on the diagonal ([EDA for Regression](note:eda-for-regression)).

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Scatterplot by occupation type - prestige on income.png
blocks.alt: Scatterplot by occupation type - prestige on income

blocks.prompt: In the grouped scatterplot, the professional occupations' line is much flatter than the blue-collar line. What does a single regression line through all 102 occupations miss?

options.md: Nothing, as long as the pooled slope is statistically significant
options.feedback: Significance of the pooled slope says that prestige rises with income on average. It cannot reveal that the rise differs across groups.

options.md: That income has no effect within professional occupations
options.feedback: The professional line is flatter, not flat: prestige still rises with income there, only more slowly.

options.md: That both the level and the slope of the prestige-income relationship differ by occupation type
That the relationship is curved within every group
options.feedback: Within each type a straight line fits reasonably; the curvature in the pooled plot comes partly from mixing groups with different lines.

blocks.why: Each colour has its own intercept and slope. One pooled line averages over them, so its slope mixes the within-type slopes with the gaps between types. The lowess bend in section 1 is partly this mixing: professionals dominate the high incomes, and their line is flatter.

blocks.md: With discrete variables many observations share the same coordinates, so a scatterplot of vocabulary score on years of education shows a grid in which one person and hundreds of people look identical. Jittering adds a little random noise to each point's plotted position, here 0.15 and then 0.3 of a unit, so the dense cells show up as clouds. The jittered plot with an OLS line and lowess shows the two nearly coinciding: the relationship is close to linear.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Vocabulary on education - jittered with OLS line and lowess.png
blocks.alt: Vocabulary on education - jittered with OLS line and lowess

blocks.prompt: The lecture jitters education and vocabulary by up to 0.3 of a unit before plotting, and adds an OLS line and a lowess curve. What does the jitter change?

options.md: The OLS estimates, slightly, because the plotted points have moved
options.feedback: The lines are fitted to the original data; the noise is added only to the plotted positions.

options.md: Only the picture: overlapping points spread out so that density becomes visible
It removes the measurement error in the discrete scores
options.feedback: Jitter adds noise to the display; it does nothing about how the scores were measured.

blocks.why: Jittering is a display device for overplotted discrete data. The fitted line and the lowess curve are computed from the unjittered values, which is why they are unchanged; the jitter only shows where the observations pile up.

sections.heading: What to be able to do

blocks.md:
1. Read a scatterplot with an OLS line and a lowess curve, and say what it means when they diverge.
2. Explain what a lowess smoother computes and how its span controls smoothness.
3. Use grouped scatterplots and a scatterplot matrix to spot differences in level and slope across groups.
4. Explain what jittering changes and what it leaves alone.
